name: Dielectric Hemorrhage Emitter DHE-4 'Blister'
description:
The DHE-4 operates by projecting a focused dielectric heating field tuned to the resonant absorption frequency of subcutaneous lipid tissue. Unlike thermal weapons that char or ignite surface material, the Blister bypasses the outer dermis almost entirely, depositing concentrated microwave-band energy into the fat and fluid layers beneath. The result is rapid steam generation inside the body — pressure builds faster than the skin can vent it, producing characteristic blistering, rupture, and in sustained exposures, catastrophic subcutaneous delamination.

What distinguishes the DHE-4 from broader-spectrum thermal emitters is its tunable penetration depth. A rotary selector on the grip adjusts the emission frequency across seven discrete bands, allowing operators to target shallow nerve clusters, mid-depth musculature, or deep organ cavities depending on the mission profile. At its shallowest setting, the weapon functions as a non-lethal pain compliance tool. At maximum depth, it is a slow, deliberate execution instrument. This range has made it simultaneously attractive to corporate security contractors and deeply controversial among humanitarian legal bodies.

ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC originally developed the DHE-4 under a medical research contract — the underlying tech was intended for non-invasive tumour ablation. When internal testing revealed its weapons potential, the project was quietly reclassified. The medical division was dissolved eighteen months later. Current production runs are manufactured under a shell subsidiary and distributed through licensed security channels, though the black market supply significantly outpaces official figures.
specifications:
effective range: 4–18 metres
penetration depth range: 2mm–14cm (frequency-dependent)
frequency bands: 7 discrete settings (2.4 GHz – 18 GHz)
power source: DHE cell cartridge (22 sustained exposures per charge)
weight: 2.1 kg
form factor: Compact emitter pistol with rotating frequency collar
heat signature: High (emitter array reaches 340°C during sustained fire)
safety interlock: Biometric grip authentication
tactical_use: Interrogation-adjacent field work, crowd dispersal at shallow settings, close-quarters anti-personnel at deep settings. Operators frequently use the shallow band to disorient armoured targets whose suits lack microwave shielding on the torso underlay. Sustained mid-band exposure through light cover (wood, plastic, thin composite) is effective — the field degrades slowly through non-metallic barriers. Metallic armour and Faraday-lined suits provide near-complete protection, which limits the weapon's utility against well-equipped military targets.
cultural_context: The Blister carries a particular stigma even in GLMZ's desensitised weapons culture. Its association with slow, internal suffering — the sound victims make, described by witnesses as 'wet and muffled' — has given it a reputation as a torturer's weapon. Corporate enforcers who carry it openly are making a specific statement about their employer's methods. In the Underbelly districts, possession of a DHE-4 is treated as evidence of affiliation with certain extraction outfits regardless of stated purpose. Some street medics have learned to reverse-engineer the shallow settings for legitimate burn treatment, which has created a strange parallel legitimacy for the device.
known_users: Rogue med-techs repurposing shallow settings for field surgery
High-end fixers with a reputation for persuasion work
"The Rendering" — an anonymous enforcer known in the Dockside district
story_hooks: A shipment of DHE-4s is traced back to a ZHENG-DAO medical subsidiary that officially doesn't exist — someone inside the corp is leaking production records and the players are hired to find out who before the whistleblower reaches a journalist.

A street medic in the Underbelly has been using a modified DHE-4 for tumour ablation on patients who can't afford clinic access. When one of her patients dies from a miscalibrated setting, she becomes the prime suspect in what looks like a targeted killing.
The players are hired to retrieve a DHE-4 prototype — frequency band 8, which doesn't appear on any public documentation — from a corporate courier who has gone off-grid.
An enforcer known for carrying a Blister has been found dead, killed by a wound pattern consistent with DHE-4 exposure. Someone used his own weapon on him and left it at the scene.
related_entities: Carrion Defense Works Field Surgical Kit FSK-6

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, brutalist pistol with an oversized emitter head dominating the front. The weapon reads as medical device crossed with industrial tool—all purposeful geometry, no ergonomic softness. A distinctive rotating collar near the grip gives it an almost mechanical, dial-like appearance. The emitter array sits proud of the slide, chunky and heat-radiating.
physical_description.dimensions: 24 cm overall length, 7 cm grip width, 5.5 cm emitter head diameter. Barrel equivalent: 8 cm forward-facing emission aperture.
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty but manageable. 2.1 kg sits forward-loaded in the hand, creating a nose-heavy balance that demands controlled aim. The weight distribution suggests serious thermal mass packed into a compact frame.
physical_description.primary_material: Titanium-reinforced polymer frame with embedded heatsink matrix. Emitter array is surgical-grade stainless steel with embedded dielectric capacitor rows. Power cell housing is brushed aluminium.
physical_description.finish: Matte charcoal polymer body with brushed steel emitter head. The frame shows deliberate surface texture to manage heat dispersal. Grip inlays are ribbed rubber with subtle iridescent copper threading for biometric contact points.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal grey and deep charcoal primary, with brushed steel highlights on the emitter and copper-toned biometric markers. Small accent stripe of warning amber runs along the frequency collar.
physical_description.grip_texture: Deeply ribbed rubberized polymer with raised copper contact nodes. Textured enough for sweaty hands, medical-cold to the touch. The frequency collar is fine-knurled stainless steel, deliberately cold and tactile for precise adjustment.
distinctive_features: Rotating frequency selector collar marked with seven discrete amber LED notches (2.4 GHz through 18 GHz in engraved microprint)
Oversized emitter head with visible dielectric grid lattice and cooling fins radiating from the aperture
Biometric grip authentication nodes (copper-toned contact patches) recessed into lower frame
Thermal bleed vents along the slide releasing shimmering heat distortion
Small ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC circular logo stamped on the trigger guard
Safety interlock lever integrated into the hammer mechanism—glows soft red when armed
Faint surgical calibration marks etched along the emitter rim (legacy medical design DNA)
Charging port (covered) on the left side of frame marked with DHE cell cartridge symbol
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC stamped subtly on the trigger guard in sans-serif block letters. Serial number laser-etched along the grip spine. Medical research-era certification stamps (now obsolete) faintly visible under the slide. No explicit branding on the emitter—just functional geometry.
physical_description.condition_typical: Corporate and black-market examples show heavy use. Emitter heads often scorched or discolored from sustained thermal cycling. Grip rubber worn shiny from heavy handling. Frequency collar sometimes chipped or seized from being adjusted under stress. Well-maintained examples retain the cold surgical finish; field-used examples show heat-stress patina and micro-pitting on the stainless emitter.
